hints: Notice option B contains $force \times displacement$ on the top line - what mechanical quantity does that product define?
Recall that power is the rate of transfer of energy, so $P = work/time$ in mechanics and $P = I^2R$ in electricity.
Compare the units needed for power, the watt, with $force \times displacement/time$ versus $weight/time$ and the two electrical forms.
walkthrough: Start from the definition of power as the rate of doing work: $P = W/t$, where $W$ is in joules and $t$ is in seconds.
Recall work done by a constant force: $W = force \times displacement$ for displacement in the direction of the force.
Combine them to get the mechanical form $P = (force \times displacement)/time$, which has units $\text{N m s}^{-1} = \text{J s}^{-1} = \text{W}$.
Check the other forms: correct Joule heating is $P = I^2R$, not $I^2/R$ or $IR^2$, and $weight/time$ omits displacement so it cannot be energy per time.
Hence $(force \times displacement)/time$ is a valid expression for power. This is option B

A.explanation: Electrical power is $(current)^2 \times resistance$, so dividing by resistance gives units of $\text{A}^2 \Omega^{-1}$ which is not power.

B.explanation: $force \times displacement$ is work done, and work divided by $time$ is the rate of doing work, which is power.

C.explanation: $current \times (resistance)^2$ has units $\text{A} \Omega^2$ and does not match $P = I^2R$ or $P = VI$.

D.explanation: $weight/time$ is $force/time$, but power needs $energy/time$, so the displacement factor is missing.
